Accessibility

Accessibility

How this site is built to be usable by everyone, what we have tested, and what we have not claimed.

Last updated 1 September 2026

BrightPath Supports provides services to people with disability. It would be a poor look if our own website were difficult to use, so accessibility is treated as part of the build rather than something checked at the end.

This page sets out what we have done, what we know is imperfect, and how to tell us when something does not work for you.

Keyboard navigation

Every interactive part of this site can be operated with a keyboard alone. Tab moves forward, Shift and Tab move back, Enter and Space activate. The navigation menus, accordions, tabs, filters and the multi-step referral form are all reachable and operable without a mouse.

A "Skip to main content" link is the first thing you reach on every page, so you do not have to tab through the whole menu to get to the content.

Focus states

Whatever you are focused on is marked with a visible outline in the same style on every page. We have not removed focus indicators anywhere, and we have not replaced them with a colour change alone, which is easy to miss.

Colour and contrast

Body text sits at a contrast ratio of at least 7:1 against its background, and no text falls below 4.5:1. Colour is never the only way information is conveyed — availability badges carry a text label and a shape as well as a colour, and form errors carry an icon and a written message.

Text size

Body text is 17px and never smaller than 15px anywhere on the site. The layout uses relative units, so the page reflows properly if you increase text size in your browser or zoom to 200 per cent.

Form labels and errors

Every field has a visible label that stays visible while you type. Hint text is linked to its field programmatically rather than sitting in the placeholder. Error messages appear next to the field, describe what to do rather than just stating that something is wrong, and are announced to screen readers.

Reduced motion

If your device is set to reduce motion, all animation is switched off — not just shortened. Scroll reveals resolve immediately, the parallax layer does not run at all, and hover movement is removed. You can set this in your operating system's accessibility settings.

Semantic markup

Pages use proper HTML landmarks — header, nav, main, footer — with one h1 per page and heading levels that descend in order. Lists are marked up as lists and buttons as buttons, so assistive technology reports the page structure accurately.

Alternative text

Images carry alternative text that describes what matters about them in context. Decorative images and icons are hidden from screen readers so they do not clutter the reading experience.

What we have not claimed

An honest note

We have built to the WCAG 2.1 Level AA guidelines and test with keyboard navigation and screen readers. We have not undergone independent certification, and we do not claim guaranteed conformance. Accessibility is a practice rather than a certificate, and there will be things we have missed.

Tell us when something does not work

If any part of this site is difficult to use, we want to know — including the small things. Ring us on 1300 555 018, email hello@brightpathsupports.com.au or use our feedback form.

We will acknowledge within two business days and tell you what we can fix and when. If we cannot fix something quickly, we will offer another way to get what you needed.

Alternative formats

Any information on this site can be provided in large print, Easy Read or as an audio recording at no cost. Interpreting and Auslan services can be arranged for meetings — tell us at enquiry rather than on the day, so we can book someone good.

Legal

Privacy Policy

What personal information we collect, why we collect it, who we share it with and how you can access or correct it.

Last updated 1 September 2026

BrightPath Supports collects personal information in order to provide disability support services. This policy explains what we collect, why, who we share it with and what you can do about it. It is written to be read rather than to be defensible, so if anything here is unclear, please ask.

We handle personal information in accordance with the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth), the Australian Privacy Principles and the NDIS Practice Standards.

What we collect

The information we collect depends on your relationship with us.

Sensitive information

Health information and disability-related information are "sensitive information" under the Privacy Act and carry stronger protections. We collect them only where necessary to deliver your supports safely, and only with your consent or where the law requires it.

How we use your information

  • To deliver the supports set out in your service agreement
  • To roster and match workers appropriately
  • To claim payment through the NDIS or from your plan manager
  • To meet our reporting obligations to the NDIS Commission
  • To investigate incidents, complaints and feedback
  • To improve our services, using de-identified information

We do not sell personal information, and we do not use it for marketing without your express consent.

Who we share it with

We share personal information only where it is necessary, and only the minimum required:

  • Support workers — the information they need to support you safely
  • The NDIA and plan managers — for claiming and plan administration
  • Health professionals — where you have consented, or in an emergency
  • The NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission — where reporting is required by law
  • Our service providers — rostering, accounting and IT systems, under written agreements

We do not disclose personal information overseas. Our systems and data are hosted in Australia.

Keeping information secure

Records are held in access-controlled systems with multi-factor authentication. Access is limited to staff whose role requires it. Paper records, where they exist, are stored in locked cabinets at our Parramatta office. Staff complete privacy training during induction and annually thereafter.

How long we keep it

Participant records are retained for seven years after supports end, or until a participant who was a child turns 25, whichever is later, as required by NDIS record-keeping rules. Unsuccessful job applications are destroyed after twelve months. Website enquiries that do not proceed are deleted after two years.

Accessing and correcting your information

You can ask to see any personal information we hold about you, and ask us to correct it if it is wrong. Email hello@brightpathsupports.com.au or ring 1300 555 018.

We will respond within 30 days. There is no charge for making a request. In rare cases we may need to refuse access — for example where it would unreasonably affect another person's privacy — and if so we will explain why in writing.

Cookies and analytics

This prototype does not set cookies, run analytics or use tracking pixels. A live deployment would require its own cookie notice, and any non-essential cookies would be off by default until you chose otherwise.

Complaints

If you think we have mishandled your personal information, tell us first — email hello@brightpathsupports.com.au and we will acknowledge within two business days.

If you are not satisfied with our response, you can complain to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner at oaic.gov.au or on 1300 363 992. You are entitled to go to them directly and we will not discourage it.

Terms of Use

The terms that apply to your use of this website, including what our information does and does not represent.

Last updated 1 September 2026

These terms apply to your use of the BrightPath Supports website. They are not your service agreement — if you receive supports from us, the terms of those supports are set out in a separate written service agreement that takes precedence over anything on this page.

1. Using this website

You may use this site to find information about our services, make an enquiry, submit a referral or apply for a role. You agree not to use it in a way that interferes with its operation, attempts to gain unauthorised access, or breaches any law.

Information on this site is general in nature. It does not take account of your individual circumstances and should not be relied on as advice — whether about the NDIS, your plan, your health or your legal rights.

NDIS rules, pricing arrangements and eligibility criteria change. While we update this site regularly, we cannot guarantee that everything is current at the moment you read it. Always confirm with us or with the NDIA before making a decision.

Nothing on this website is medical, clinical or allied health advice. We are a disability support provider, not a health service. If you have a health concern, speak to your GP or the relevant health professional. In an emergency, call 000.

BrightPath Supports is a registered NDIS provider. Registration means we have been audited against the NDIS Practice Standards. We aim to keep this site available at all times but we do not guarantee uninterrupted access. We may suspend access for maintenance, and we may change or remove content without notice.

To the extent permitted by law, we exclude liability for any loss arising from your use of this website or reliance on its content. Nothing in these terms excludes rights you have under the Australian Consumer Law that cannot lawfully be excluded.

We may update these terms from time to time. The current version is always on this page with the date it was last updated. Continuing to use the site after a change means you accept the updated terms.

These terms are governed by the laws of New South Wales, Australia, and you submit to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of that state.

posts.content:
About us

Support built on turning up.

BrightPath Supports has provided NDIS services across Greater Sydney since 2016. We are not the biggest provider in the state and we are not trying to be.

Team Portrait — BrightPath Supports

Operating since

Who we are

A provider that fits around people, not rosters.

We support more than 280 participants across eight regions of Greater Sydney, with a team of around 140 support workers. Most of them live in the suburbs where they work, which is not an accident — it is the single thing that makes reliable support possible.

Our services span daily living, community participation, supported independent living, respite, coordination, transport, life skills and in-home support. Participants commonly use two or three together, on one roster, with one point of contact.

We are a registered NDIS provider and we work with self-managed, plan-managed and NDIA-managed participants.

Support Worker and Participant Outdoors

Our story

It started with a roster that made no sense.

In 2016 Marisa Vong was a team leader at a large provider in Western Sydney. One of the participants she supported, a man in his thirties who worked Saturday mornings at a hardware store, kept being rostered support at 9am on Saturdays. He asked four times to move it. The roster did not move, because the roster was built around staff availability rather than around him. Eventually he stopped going to work.

Marisa left three months later and started BrightPath from her lounge room in Parramatta with one other support worker and four participants. The operating principle was simple and has not changed: the roster bends around the person.

Ten years on we are a team of 140 across eight regions. The business has grown in ways we did not plan — SIL homes, a coordination team, a training programme. What has not changed is that every new participant is asked the same first question. What does a good week look like for you?

We still get things wrong. When we do, we say so, fix it, and write down what we learned. That is the whole method.

Our mission

To provide NDIS supports that fit around the lives people actually lead — reliable, respectful, and shaped by the person receiving them rather than the organisation delivering them.

Our vision

A Sydney where disabled people choose their support with the same ease anyone else chooses a service — and where "we will have to check the roster" is never the answer to a reasonable request.

What we stand for

Six things we actually do

Values are only worth writing down if they change a decision. These ones do.

You are in charge

Every decision about your support is yours to make. Our job is to give you real options and honest information, not to steer you.

Say the hard thing kindly

If we cannot deliver something, if a match is not working, or if another provider suits you better, we will tell you.

Show up

Reliability is the whole job. A brilliant support worker who is late twice a week is not a brilliant support worker.

Everyone belongs

All abilities, cultures, genders, sexualities and faiths. Workers matched on language and culture wherever we can.

Aim to be needed less

Good support builds capability. If you need fewer hours from us next year, that is a result we are proud of.

Safety is not paperwork

Safeguarding is a daily practice, not an annual audit. Everyone here knows how to raise a concern.

Our people

Meet the team

A small leadership team, a large field team, and a deliberate policy of keeping the gap between them narrow.

Meet everyone

Team Training Session

Quality and safeguarding

The unglamorous part, done properly.

Safeguarding only works when it is ordinary. Ours is built into weekly routine rather than saved up for audit season.

  • Registered NDIS provider, audited against the NDIS Practice Standards
  • NDIS Worker Screening Check and Working with Children Check for every worker
  • Mandatory training in safeguarding, manual handling and infection control
  • Incident reporting reviewed weekly by the Service Manager
  • Participant feedback and complaints acknowledged within two business days
  • Behaviour support plans written by qualified practitioners and reviewed six-monthly
Give feedback
Read our accessibility statement

If something goes wrong, you can raise it with any staff member, through our feedback form, or directly with the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission. We will never discourage you from doing the latter.

Services

Funding

Yes. We charge within the NDIS Pricing Arrangements and Price Limits, and your service agreement sets out the rate for each support item before you sign. There are no administration fees on top of the published rates.

We monitor your budget alongside you and will flag it well before it becomes a problem. If funding is running short we can help you apply for a plan review, or adjust the roster so what remains lasts the plan period.

Short-notice cancellations may be charged in line with the NDIS Pricing Arrangements, which currently allow a charge when less than seven days' notice is given. We apply this sparingly and never for illness, hospital admission or circumstances outside your control.

Supported Living

SIL funds the support workers who help you in the home. SDA funds the building itself, where housing is specially designed for high support needs. Many participants have SIL only; some have both.

Yes. We arrange meet-ups before anyone commits — usually a coffee first, then a visit to the house, then often an overnight stay. Nobody moves in on the strength of a profile on paper.

We work through it with you, your family and your coordinator. Sometimes it is a roster change or a house agreement conversation. If a move is genuinely the right answer, we help you find something better.

Referrals

Support coordinators, plan managers, health professionals, family members, guardians — or participants themselves. We need the participant's consent, or their legally appointed decision maker's, before we can act on it.

We acknowledge every referral within one business day and confirm capacity, suitability and an indicative start date within two. If we cannot take a referral we will say so quickly rather than leaving it sitting.

Working With Us

An NDIS Worker Screening Check and a Working with Children Check before your first shift. We cover the cost of both. You will also need First Aid and CPR, which we will fund if you do not already have it.

posts.content:
Supported Independent Living

A place to live. Support to live your way.

Ordinary homes in ordinary streets, with the right level of support and housemates you have actually met. Across Parramatta, Blacktown, Penrith, Liverpool, Bankstown, the Hills, the Inner West and Western Sydney.

Browse SIL homes
Make a referral

SIL Home Exterior — Street View

The basics

What is Supported Independent Living?

SIL is NDIS funding for the support you receive inside your home. It covers the workers who help with personal care, meals, medication and household tasks — including overnight, where your plan funds it.

It is worth being clear about what SIL is not. SIL does not pay for the house. Rent or board comes out of your own income, the same as it would for anyone renting. And SIL is not a facility: our homes are regular houses on regular streets, with neighbours who mow their lawns on Sunday.

For most people SIL means sharing with one to three housemates, because pooled support hours stretch further. Individual living options exist too, and we will tell you honestly which your funding is likely to support.

Who SIL may suit

  • You are moving out of the family home for the first time
  • You are leaving hospital or a rehabilitation setting
  • Your current living arrangement is no longer working
  • You need support available overnight
  • You want your own tenancy with support that comes to you
  • Your informal supports are changing and you need a stable base

SIL Home Interior — Kitchen and Dining

Our approach

A house runs on the people in it.

The building matters far less than most brochures suggest. What determines whether a home works is whether the housemates get along, whether the staff stay, and whether anyone asks your opinion about how things are run.

  • Dedicated team per home, not a floating pool
  • Monthly house meetings with participant-led agendas
  • Written house agreements made together, not handed down
  • Behaviour support plans developed with qualified practitioners

So we roster small, consistent teams to each house rather than rotating whoever is available. House meetings happen monthly and participants set the agenda. And we say no to a placement when the match is wrong, even when the bed is empty and the referral is sitting in front of us.

What's included

Support that comes with the home

The exact mix depends on what your plan funds and what you actually want help with.

✓

Daily household support

Cooking, cleaning, shopping and running the house together.

✓

Personal care

In your own bathroom, on your own schedule.

✓

Overnight support

Active night or sleepover cover, depending on your plan.

✓

Medication management

Systems, records and staff trained to your health plan.

✓

Skill building

Cooking, budgeting and household routines at your pace.

✓

Community connection

Support to stay linked with family, friends and activities.

Resident matching

How we match people to homes

We talk through what you are looking for, what your plan funds and what your non-negotiables are.

Assessment visit

We meet you where you are now, with family or your coordinator if you would like them there.

03

Shortlist and visits

We show you the homes that genuinely fit, and you visit as many times as you want.

04

Meet your housemates

Coffee first, then a house visit, then usually an overnight or weekend stay.

05

Confirm and move in

Funding confirmed, agreements signed, and we help with the practical side of moving.

Questions

About Supported Independent Living

SIL pays for the support workers who assist you in the home — help with personal care, meals, medication, household tasks and overnight support. It does not pay your rent or board. Those are paid from your own income, usually from the Disability Support Pension, in the same way any tenant pays rent.

No. Most of our homes are shared with one to three housemates because it makes support hours go further, but we also have individual living options where you have your own self-contained space with support available nearby.

We look at daily routines, noise and quiet preferences, interests, communication styles and support needs. Then we arrange a coffee, then a visit to the house, then usually an overnight or weekend stay. Nobody signs anything until everyone has met.

Of course. It is your home. Visitors are welcome, and there is nothing unusual about family staying for a meal. We ask housemates to agree some basic ground rules together so everyone gets reasonable notice and quiet time.

You can. Your residency agreement sets out the notice period, usually four weeks. We will support the transition, including helping you look at other options, whether they are ours or another provider's.

From first enquiry to moving in is commonly six to twelve weeks. That covers the assessment, matching, house visits, funding confirmation with the NDIA and the practical business of moving. We will give you a realistic timeline at the first conversation, not an optimistic one.

posts.title: Careers
posts.content:
Careers

Make a difference doing work that matters.

We are hiring support workers, team leaders and coordinators across Greater Sydney. Above-award pay, rosters you can plan around, and a team leader who picks up the phone.

View open roles
Register your interest

Careers Image — Support Worker Team

Why work with us

The sector has a retention problem. We decided not to have one.

Support work is hard to do well and easy to do badly, and most of the difference comes down to whether the organisation behind the worker is any good. Too many providers run on unpaid travel, rosters published on a Friday night, and a phone number nobody answers at 6am when a shift falls over.

  • Paid induction before your first shift, not learning on the job
  • Consistent participants, so you build real relationships
  • Someone reachable during every shift

We built BrightPath the other way round, because consistent workers are the single thing participants ask for most. Our average support worker has been with us for three and a half years. In this sector that is unusual, and it is not an accident.

Support Worker on Shift

Benefits

What you actually get

Not a fruit bowl and a foosball table. The things that determine whether this job is sustainable.

Above-award pay

We pay above the SCHADS Award minimum at every level, with penalty rates on evenings, weekends and public holidays.

Rosters you can plan around

Published a fortnight ahead and built from the availability you give us, not the other way round.

Paid travel

Travel time between shifts is paid and kilometres are reimbursed at the ATO rate.

Real training budget

Paid induction and ongoing professional development during working hours, funded by us.

A team leader who answers

Every worker has a regional team leader who is reachable during shifts. Not a portal, a person.

Career progression

Senior support worker, team leader and coordinator roles are filled from within wherever we can.

Team Culture — Staff Debrief

Culture

Small enough that people know your name.

We are 140 support workers across eight regions, with regional teams small enough that your team leader knows what you are good at and what you would rather not do.

Debriefs happen after hard shifts, not weeks later. Ideas from the field reach the director, and several of our current policies started as a suggestion from someone on the floor. Nobody is expected to absorb difficult things alone.

We also recruit deliberately for diversity of language, culture and lived experience, because our participants are diverse and matching matters.

Open roles

Current jobs

Six roles open across Sydney. We also accept expressions of interest when nothing listed suits.

Register your interest

◆

Hiring process

From application to first shift

Usually two to three weeks, most of which is waiting on screening checks.

01

Apply online

A short form and your resume. No cover letter required — we would rather read about you than a template.

02

Phone chat

Fifteen minutes with our people team to talk through availability and what you are looking for.

03

Interview

In person at one of our offices, or by video if that suits better. Practical scenarios, not trick questions.

04

Checks and induction

Screening checks, references, then a paid two-day induction before your first shift.

Questions

Working at BrightPath

Not to apply. A Certificate III in Individual Support helps, but plenty of our best workers came from hospitality, retail or aged care with no formal qualification. What you do need is a current driver's licence, the right to work in Australia and the willingness to complete our paid induction.

An NDIS Worker Screening Check and a Working with Children Check before your first shift. We cover the cost of both and help you through the applications. You will also need a First Aid and CPR certificate, which we will pay for if you do not already have one.

You tell us your availability and we roster to it. Rosters are published a fortnight ahead. Casual staff can decline shifts without any consequence — we would rather know early than have someone turn up resentful.

Yes. Travel time between consecutive shifts is paid, and kilometres are reimbursed at the ATO rate. Travel from home to your first shift is not paid, which is standard across the sector.

A paid two-day induction covering manual handling, safeguarding, infection control and our systems. After that, ongoing training in areas like positive behaviour support, medication administration, epilepsy management and Auslan basics — all funded by us and completed during paid hours.

Ready to apply?

Send us a short application and your resume. No cover letter needed — we would rather hear about you in a conversation.

What this support actually looks like

Assistance with daily living covers the parts of the day that have to happen: getting up, getting washed and dressed, eating well, taking medication and getting out the door on time. How much support you want is entirely your call, and it can change from day to day.

Our workers are trained in personal care and manual handling, but the thing participants mention most often is far simpler — the same person turns up, they know your routine, and they do not rush you.

Who this may suit

  • You need a hand with personal care in the morning or evening
  • Meal preparation has become difficult or unsafe
  • You want medication prompts without someone taking over
  • You are moving into your own place and building a routine
  • A family carer needs regular, reliable backup

What is included

What support can include

✓

Showering, dressing, grooming, continence support and transfers, delivered with dignity and privacy.

Planning, shopping, cooking together or preparing ahead — including cultural and dietary needs.

✓

Reminders and supervision in line with your plan and your GP's instructions.

✓

Around the home

Laundry, tidying, changing linen and keeping the space safe to move through.

✓

Morning and evening routines

Early starts, late finishes and overnight support where it is funded.

✓

Help with appointments, phone calls and correspondence when you want it.

Community participation is about doing the things you would do anyway if getting there was simpler. That might be a weekly art class, a footy game, a swim, a shift at the local op shop, or just a coffee with someone who is good company.

We start by asking what you actually enjoy, not what programmes we happen to run. Then we work out the transport, the access and the support you need to make it happen regularly rather than once.

  • You are looking to build a social circle outside the house

Introduction

What this support actually looks like

Transport is the support that quietly unlocks everything else. If getting there is unreliable, the appointment gets missed, the shift gets dropped and the invitation stops coming.

We provide door-to-door travel with a support worker, and we also do travel training — practising a route until you can do it on your own. Plenty of participants start with the first and move to the second.

Who this may suit

  • Public transport is not accessible on your route
  • You need support during the journey, not just at either end
  • Appointments are spread across Sydney and hard to link up
  • You want to learn a route so you can travel independently
  • You need reliable travel to a job or a course

Life skills support is about doing less for you over time, not more. We work on the specific skills that would make the biggest difference to your week, break them into steps, and practise until they stick.

Progress is tracked in plain language so you can see it, and so it is there as evidence at your next plan review. Small, boring, repeated wins are how this works.

A support coordinator helps you turn a plan document into supports that actually run. That means explaining what each budget covers, finding providers with real capacity, setting up service agreements and following up when something is not working.

We work with you, not around you. You choose the providers; we do the ringing around, the comparing and the chasing. If you would rather learn to do it yourself, we will teach you that instead — the goal is for you to need us less.

The plan is three budgets, not one pot of money, and most of the confusion people bring to us is about which budget pays for what.

Core supports

Capacity building

Skill building with a goal attached. Less flexible than core: the money is allocated against the goal it was approved for.

Capital supports

Equipment, home modifications and assistive technology. The least flexible, and usually quoted.

posts.title: What SIL funding actually pays for
posts.content:
Every week someone rings us having just read their plan, and asks a version of the same question: it says SIL, so does that mean my housing is paid for? The short answer is no, and the longer answer is worth five minutes of your time because it shapes what you can realistically plan for.

What SIL actually funds

Supported Independent Living funds the support workers who assist you in your home. That is the whole of it. The hours they work, the tasks they do, the overnight cover — all support, all funded through SIL.

In practice, SIL typically covers:

  • Help with personal care — showering, dressing, transfers
  • Support with meals, from planning through to cooking together
  • Medication prompting and supervision
  • Household tasks done alongside you
  • Overnight support, either sleepover or active night
  • Support to build skills like cooking and budgeting

A useful way to think about it

SIL pays for people, not property. If it is a person helping you, it is probably SIL. If it is a building, a ramp or a rent payment, it is not.

SIL is not SDA

Specialist Disability Accommodation is a separate payment, and it does relate to the building. SDA funds housing that has been specifically designed or modified for people with extreme functional impairment or very high support needs — reinforced walls, ceiling hoists, fully accessible bathrooms, robust construction.

Only a small proportion of participants are eligible for SDA, roughly six per cent nationally. Most people living in supported accommodation have SIL funding and live in ordinary rental housing.

Some participants have both: SDA pays the specialist housing provider for the dwelling, and SIL pays the support provider for the workers. They are commonly two different organisations, which is deliberate — it means you can change your support provider without losing your home.

So who pays the rent?

You do, from your own income. For most participants that means the Disability Support Pension, and the expectation is that you contribute roughly the same proportion of your income to rent and living costs as anyone else would.

You will usually pay a reasonable rent contribution — commonly around 25 per cent of the Disability Support Pension plus the full Commonwealth Rent Assistance — together with a share of household costs such as electricity, internet and groceries. Exact figures vary by arrangement, and any provider should show you a written breakdown before you sign.

How much SIL funding will I get?

SIL funding is based on your assessed support needs, not on the house you want to live in. The NDIA looks at how many hours of support you need, at what times, at what ratio of workers to participants, and whether overnight support is active or sleepover.

Sharing with others generally stretches funding further, because some support hours are shared across the household. That is the practical reason most SIL arrangements involve housemates.

The question to ask is not “how much SIL funding can I get?” but “what does my week actually need to look like, and what support does that require?” Build the case from the week backwards.

Getting SIL into your plan

SIL is not automatically included. You will generally need a roster of care — a document setting out, hour by hour, what support you need across a typical week — along with evidence from your allied health team about your functional capacity.

Most providers will help prepare a roster of care at no cost, including us. It is worth having more than one prepared if you are considering different living arrangements.

Questions worth asking a provider

  • What exactly will I pay each fortnight, in writing, including all household costs?
  • Who owns or leases the property, and what happens to my tenancy if I change support provider?
  • How are housemates matched, and can I meet them before deciding?
  • What is the staff turnover in this house over the past year?
  • What happens if the arrangement is not working after six months?

A provider who cannot answer the second and fourth questions clearly is worth a second look. Neither is unreasonable, and both tell you a lot.

Need a hand with any of this?

Our coordinators can prepare a roster of care and talk through what your plan is likely to support — whether or not you end up choosing us as a provider.

posts.title: Preparing for your plan review
posts.content:
A plan review can feel like an exam you did not study for. In reality it is a conversation about how the last plan went and what you need next. The people who come out of it with a plan that fits are rarely the ones with the most paperwork. They are the ones who started early, kept it simple, and linked every request back to their goals.

Why the review matters

Your plan sets out the supports the NDIA considers reasonable and necessary for you. A review is the point where that is checked against how your life actually looks now. If your needs have changed, if a support has not worked, or if you have new goals, this is your chance to say so with evidence behind it.

It is also a chance to keep what is working. If a support has made a real difference, say that clearly. Continuity is worth arguing for.

Evidence worth gathering

Good evidence describes what you can and cannot do day to day, and what difference support makes. It does not need to be long. Useful items include:

  • Recent reports from your treating professionals, such as an occupational therapist, physiotherapist or psychologist
  • Progress notes or summaries from your current providers
  • A short statement in your own words about how the last plan went
  • Notes from family or carers about the support they provide and how sustainable it is
  • Any assessments completed since your last plan, including equipment or home modification assessments

Ask your providers early. Allied health reports in particular can take several weeks to write, and a report that arrives after the meeting cannot help you.

Keep it about your life, not the diagnosis

The NDIA already knows your diagnosis. What helps is a clear picture of how it affects your week, and what support lets you do.

Language that helps

You do not need special wording, but some habits make your case easier to follow. Tie each request to a goal in your plan. Describe function rather than labels: “I need someone with me to shower safely” says more than “high needs”. Be specific about frequency and time, such as how many days a week and how many hours each time.

Be honest about bad days as well as good ones. Many people describe their best day in a meeting because it feels more comfortable. Your plan needs to cover your harder days too.

The six-week timeline we recommend

Here is the rough rhythm we use with participants. Adjust it to suit you, but try to leave room at the end.

  1. Six weeks out: check your plan end date, re-read your goals, and ask providers and therapists for reports.
  2. Five weeks out: look at how your budget has been used. Note anything that ran short or went unused, and why.
  3. Four weeks out: write your own statement. A page is plenty.
  4. Three weeks out: follow up any reports that have not arrived.
  5. Two weeks out: put everything in one folder and list the changes you are asking for.
  6. The week of the meeting: decide who will come with you, and have your list of questions ready.

On the day

Bring someone you trust if that helps: a family member, friend, advocate or your support coordinator. Take notes, or ask your support person to. If you do not understand something, ask for it to be explained. It is reasonable to ask what happens next and roughly when you can expect your new plan.

If the new plan does not fit

Read the new plan carefully when it arrives and compare it with what you asked for. If something important is missing or does not reflect your needs, you can ask the NDIA to look at the decision again. There are time limits for this, so do not leave it. Your support coordinator or a disability advocate can help you work out the next step.

Want a hand getting ready?

Our coordinators help participants prepare for reviews every week, from chasing reports to writing a short statement that says what you need.

Want to talk it through? Request support or call 1300 555 018 and one of our coordinators will help.

posts.title: How to choose a support worker who suits you
posts.content:
Most people choose a support worker on the basis of who is free on Tuesday afternoons. Availability matters, but it is only the starting point. The support worker you see most often will be in your home, in your routine and sometimes in your most personal moments. It is worth taking the time to get the match right.

Start with what matters to you

Before you talk to any provider, write down what a good support session looks like for you. Think about the tasks, but also the feel of it. Some people want someone chatty; others want someone calm and quiet. Some want a worker who takes the lead; others want someone who waits to be asked.

  • The tasks you need help with, and the ones you would rather do yourself
  • Days and times, and how much flexibility you need
  • Interests you would like to share, such as sport, music, cooking or gaming
  • Language, culture or gender preferences
  • Anything that is a firm no for you

Your preferences are reasonable

Asking for a worker of a particular gender for personal care, or someone who speaks your language, is not being fussy. It is part of getting support that works.

Questions to ask a provider

A good provider will be glad you asked. Try these:

  • How do you match workers to participants, beyond availability?
  • Can I meet a worker before the first shift?
  • What training and screening do your workers have?
  • Who will cover when my regular worker is on leave or unwell?
  • How do I raise a concern, and who do I speak to?
  • How often will my worker change?

Listen for specific answers. “We find the best person for you” is nice to hear, but it does not tell you much.

The first few shifts

The first few weeks are a settling-in period for both of you. Expect some awkwardness while your worker learns how you like things done. Tell them early and plainly. Small things, such as where the cups go or how you like to be woken, are much easier to sort out in week one than in month six.

It can help to write a short “about me” page covering your routine, likes and dislikes, and what to do if you are unwell or upset. Many people find this saves them repeating themselves every time a new worker starts.

When the match is not working

Sometimes, despite everyone’s best efforts, a match just does not work. That is nobody’s failure. Signs it may be time for a change include:

  • You dread shifts or feel uncomfortable with the worker
  • Your preferences are repeatedly ignored
  • You feel rushed, talked over or not listened to
  • Your goals are not moving forward

Start by talking to your provider’s coordinator or team leader. You can ask for a different worker without giving a long explanation. If you do not feel comfortable raising it yourself, a family member, advocate or your support coordinator can do it with you.

If you feel unsafe, or you think a worker has behaved in a way that is not okay, raise it straight away. Every registered NDIS provider must have a complaints process, and you can also contact the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission.

Keeping a good match going

When you find a worker who suits you, look after the relationship. Give feedback, including the good kind. Tell your provider what is working so they protect that roster where they can. Continuity is one of the most valuable things a provider can offer, and you are allowed to ask for it.

Looking for a better fit?

We match support workers on more than availability. Tell us what matters to you and we will talk through who might suit.

posts.title: A coordinator’s guide to referring well
posts.content:
Every provider has a pile of referrals. The ones that move quickly are not always the most urgent. They are the ones that are complete. A clear referral lets a provider work out, in one read, whether they can safely support someone and when. A vague one leads to a round of emails, and meanwhile the participant waits.

What a provider needs to decide

When we receive a referral, we are trying to answer three questions: can we meet this person’s needs safely, do we have capacity at the times they need, and is the funding in place to support it. Everything in a good referral helps answer one of those.

The essentials

  • Participant name, contact details and preferred contact method
  • Who else should be contacted, such as a nominee, guardian or family member, and their consent to be involved
  • The supports requested, with days, times and frequency
  • Location, including suburb and any access considerations
  • Plan dates, how the plan is managed, and the relevant budget
  • Key goals from the plan that this support relates to
  • Any communication needs or preferences
  • Known risks, including behaviours of concern, health needs or mealtime management

Consent first

Make sure the participant has agreed to the referral and to their information being shared. It sounds obvious, but it is the most common reason we have to pause.

Why vague referrals sit at the bottom

A referral that says “needs support, flexible, ASAP” is hard to act on. A provider cannot roster a worker, check skills or confirm funding from it. It is not that anyone ignores it. It is that it needs more work before anyone can say yes, and the complete referrals get answered first.

Be especially clear about risk. Leaving out a behaviour support plan or a complex health need does not help the participant. It means the provider may say yes to something they cannot safely deliver, and the arrangement breaks down a few weeks later.

Attachments that help

You do not need to send everything. The most useful documents are usually:

  • The relevant pages of the NDIS plan, particularly goals and budgets
  • A behaviour support plan, if there is one
  • Recent allied health reports that describe function and support needs
  • Mealtime management or health care plans, where relevant
  • For accommodation referrals, a roster of care or a description of the support needed across the week

Setting expectations with the participant

Let the participant and family know what happens next. A provider may need to meet the person, check the home, or confirm worker availability before offering a start date. Explaining that early saves anxious phone calls and helps everyone understand that a short wait is normal.

A short summary at the top of the referral also helps. Two or three sentences about who the person is, what they enjoy and what they are hoping support will change gives a provider a sense of the person, not just the paperwork. It also helps us think about which worker or home might suit, before we have even met. If the participant has written something themselves, include it, even if it is brief.

If you are referring to several providers at once, say so. It is common practice, and it helps providers understand the timing.

Following up well

If you have not heard back within the time a provider says they respond, follow up once, politely, with the participant’s name and the date of the referral. If a provider declines, ask why. The reason is often useful, whether it is capacity in a certain area or a skill mix they do not have right now.

Referring to BrightPath?

Our referral form asks for exactly what we need. We confirm capacity, suitability and an indicative start date within two business days.

posts.title: Changes to NDIS pricing from July
posts.content:
Each year the NDIA reviews its Pricing Arrangements and Price Limits, and updates usually take effect from 1 July. For most participants the changes are small and happen in the background. But it is worth understanding what they mean, particularly if you have service agreements already in place.

What the Pricing Arrangements are

The NDIS Pricing Arrangements and Price Limits is a document published by the NDIA. It sets the maximum prices that registered providers can charge for many supports, and explains the rules around things like travel, cancellations and non-face-to-face time.

The key word is maximum. A price limit is a ceiling, not a set price. Providers can charge less, and some do.

Where to find the official detail

The current Pricing Arrangements are published on the NDIS website. If you are unsure how a change affects a particular support, check the source document or ask your plan manager.

What typically changes each July

The annual review can touch different areas from year to year. Commonly it involves:

  • Updates to price limits for some support items
  • Changes to support item names, numbers or descriptions
  • Clarifications to rules such as short notice cancellations or provider travel
  • Changes to how certain supports are claimed

Sometimes the NDIA also publishes guidance or questions and answers alongside the new Pricing Arrangements. These can be useful if a change is not clear from the main document. Changes are generally announced ahead of 1 July, which gives providers and participants some time to prepare, but it is still worth checking your agreements in June so there are no surprises in your first invoices of the new financial year.

Not every support changes every year. Some price limits may stay the same.

What it means for your agreed supports

If you have a service agreement, check what it says about price changes. Many agreements explain that prices may be updated in line with the Pricing Arrangements, and how much notice the provider will give. A provider should tell you about any change to what they charge you before it applies.

Your plan budget does not automatically grow when prices change. If prices go up, the same budget may stretch a little less far. It is worth keeping an eye on how your funding is tracking over the rest of the plan.

Questions to ask your providers

  • Are your prices changing from July, and for which supports?
  • Will you send me an updated schedule of supports?
  • Does my service agreement need to be updated or re-signed?
  • Will this change how many hours my budget will cover?

If you self-manage or use a plan manager

If your plan is plan-managed, your plan manager will generally check that invoices from registered providers sit within the current price limits. If you self-manage, it is worth reading the parts of the Pricing Arrangements relevant to the supports you buy, and checking invoices against your agreements.

If something looks wrong on an invoice, ask the provider first. Most errors are simple and quickly fixed.

How we handle changes at BrightPath

When the Pricing Arrangements change, we review our prices and write to participants and plan managers before any change applies. If your service agreement needs updating, we will explain what has changed in plain language and give you time to ask questions. Nothing changes on your roster just because prices have been updated.

Not sure how this affects your plan?

Our team can walk through your current agreement with you and explain what, if anything, is changing.

posts.title: BrightPath opens a new home in Castle Hill
posts.content:
We are pleased to share that BrightPath has opened a new Supported Independent Living home in Castle Hill, in Sydney’s Hills District. The four-bedroom home has been set up with accessibility in mind, and we have two vacancies from October.

About the home

The home is a four-bedroom house in a residential street in Castle Hill. Each resident has their own bedroom, with shared living, dining and kitchen spaces. It has been chosen and set up to be accessible, so that people can move around their home as independently as possible.

As with all our homes, the aim is for it to feel like a home rather than a service. Residents are encouraged to decorate their own rooms and to have a say in how the household runs.

Why the Hills District

Many of the people we support already live in or have family in north-west Sydney. A home in Castle Hill means people can stay close to the family, friends, work, study and community groups that already matter to them, rather than moving across the city to find a vacancy.

Staying connected

Being close to your existing community is one of the things we weigh most carefully when matching people to a home.

Who the home may suit

The home may suit adults with SIL funding in their plan who are looking to live with a small group of housemates, with support available day to day. Every household is different, so we take time to understand each person’s needs, routines and preferences before talking about fit.

  • People looking to move out of the family home for the first time
  • People wanting to live closer to family in north-west Sydney
  • People whose current living arrangement is no longer meeting their needs

How we match housemates

Sharing a home is a big decision, and getting the mix right matters for everyone. Before anyone moves in, we look at routines, interests, support needs and personalities. Prospective residents are welcome to visit the home and, where current residents agree, meet the people they may be living with.

We also think about the support team. Residents in the Castle Hill home will be supported by a consistent group of workers led by a house coordinator, so people get to know the faces around them. Families are welcome to be involved in the transition, and we plan moves gradually where that suits the person, with visits, a meal or two and perhaps an overnight stay before the move itself.

We would rather take a little longer to find the right match than fill a room quickly with someone who will not be happy there.

How to express interest

If you, a family member or someone you support may be interested, the first step is a conversation. It helps to have the following ready:

  • A copy of the current NDIS plan, or details of the SIL funding if it is being applied for
  • A short description of the support needed across a typical week
  • Any relevant reports, such as allied health or behaviour support plans
  • Preferred move-in timing

Support coordinators can refer directly through our referral form. We will confirm capacity, suitability and an indicative start date within two business days.

Thank you

Opening a new home takes the work of many people, from our house team to the families who have shared what matters to them. We look forward to welcoming the first residents and to the home becoming part of the neighbourhood.

posts.title: Travel training: from the first trip to travelling alone
posts.content:
Being able to get yourself from A to B opens up a lot: work, study, friends, appointments and the simple freedom of deciding to go somewhere. Travel training is how many people get there. It is practical, it is gradual, and it looks different for everyone.

What travel training is

Travel training is support to learn how to use public transport, or to travel on foot, safely and with growing independence. A support worker travels with you at first, then gradually steps back as your confidence and skills build. The goal is for you to make a specific trip, or trips, on your own.

Depending on your plan, travel training may be funded as part of capacity building supports. Your support coordinator or plan manager can help you check where it fits in your budget.

Starting with one trip

Good travel training starts with one real trip that matters to you, such as getting to work, TAFE, a day program or a friend’s place. Practising a trip you actually need keeps motivation high and makes each session count.

  • Where are you going, and why does it matter to you?
  • What transport is involved: walking, bus, train, or a mix?
  • What time of day will you usually travel?
  • What worries you most about the trip?

How it works in practice

Most travel training moves through similar stages, though the pace is yours:

  1. Travelling together: your worker does the trip with you, talking through each step, from checking the timetable to tapping on with your Opal card.
  2. You lead, they follow: you make the decisions while your worker stays close by.
  3. Distance support: your worker travels separately, perhaps on the same bus but a few seats away, or meets you at the destination.
  4. Travelling alone: you make the trip independently, often with a check-in call or message at first.

Planning for the unexpected

Good training includes what to do when things go wrong: a cancelled service, a missed stop, a lost card or a phone with a flat battery. Practise these as well as the smooth days.

How long it takes

Honestly, it depends. Some people are confident on a familiar trip within a few weeks. For others, especially where a trip involves changes between services or busy stations, it can take a few months. Progress is not always a straight line. A bad day, a timetable change or a new route can mean stepping back for a while, and that is normal.

Your worker will usually keep simple notes on each session, such as which steps you managed on your own and which still need support. Reviewing these together every few weeks helps you see how far you have come, and helps everyone decide when it is time to step back a little more. These notes can also be useful evidence at your next plan review.

What matters is steady progress towards the trip you want to make, not how quickly you get there.

Tools that help

  • A written or picture-based step-by-step guide for the trip
  • Transport apps with real-time updates
  • A card with key contact numbers
  • An agreed plan for checking in with family or your worker

For families

It is natural to feel nervous about someone you love travelling alone. Being involved in planning, knowing the route and agreeing on a check-in routine can help. Building independence always involves some reasonable risk, and a well-planned approach helps keep that risk manageable.

Ready to start?

Our Transport Assistance and Life Skills teams can build a travel training plan around the trip that matters most to you.

Want to talk it through? Request support or call 1300 555 018 and one of our coordinators will help.

posts.title: Talking to your family about moving out
posts.content:
For many people, moving out of the family home is one of the biggest steps they will take. For families, it can bring pride, worry, relief and grief all at once. Starting the conversation about Supported Independent Living can feel hard, but it tends to go better with a little planning.

Why the conversation feels hard

Families have often been the main support for years. Talking about moving out can feel like saying that support was not good enough, or raise fears about what happens next. For the person moving, there may be worry about hurting feelings, or about whether they will cope.

Naming this can help. Moving out is usually not about anything going wrong at home. It is about growing up, building independence and planning for the long term.

A normal step

Most adults move out of their family home at some point. Wanting the same is not a rejection of your family.

Choosing the right moment

Pick a calm time, not in the middle of a disagreement or a busy morning. Some people find it easier to talk while doing something together, like going for a walk or a drive. You do not need to cover everything at once. The first conversation can simply be: “I have been thinking about moving out one day. Can we talk about it?”

Ways to start that tend to go better

  • Start with what you want your life to look like, not with the house
  • Talk about the future rather than problems with the present
  • Ask for their thoughts and worries, and listen to the answers
  • Invite them to be part of the planning
  • Suggest looking into it together, with no decision needed yet

If you are a parent raising it with your adult child, the same ideas apply in reverse. Ask what they hope for, and be open about why you are thinking about it, including planning for a time when you may not be able to provide the same support.

Common worries, and what helps

Families often worry about safety, the quality of support, and whether their family member will be lonely. Practical information helps with most of these. Visit homes together, ask providers how they match housemates and handle concerns, and ask what contact with family looks like after the move.

It is also fine for family members to have their own feelings about the change, and to want some support with them. Some families find it helpful to talk with other parents who have been through a move, or with a counsellor. Looking after the whole family makes it easier for everyone to support the person who is moving.

It can also help to know that moving out does not end the family relationship. Many families say that once day-to-day support is shared, time together becomes more about enjoying each other.

Getting support to plan

You do not have to work it out alone. A support coordinator can explain how SIL works, what evidence may be needed in the plan, and what the options look like. Some people try a stay in Short Term Accommodation first, to get a feel for living away from home before making a bigger decision.

  • Talk to your support coordinator about your goals
  • Check whether your plan includes, or could include, SIL funding
  • Visit a few homes and meet providers
  • Consider a trial stay if it is available to you

Taking it one step at a time

This is rarely one conversation. It is usually many, over months. That is fine. Each conversation builds a little more understanding, and the final decision should be one the person moving feels good about.

Want to talk it through as a family?

Our coordinators are happy to sit down with you and your family to explain the options, with no pressure to decide anything.

Want to talk it through? Request support or call 1300 555 018 and one of our coordinators will help.

posts.title: Support Worker — Parramatta
posts.content:
Role overview

We are looking for casual support workers to join our Parramatta team, supporting participants with daily living, community access and in-home support across Parramatta, Harris Park, Westmead and Granville.

You will work with a small, consistent group of participants rather than a different person every shift. Most of our casual workers build up to a regular pattern within a couple of months, and many move to part-time hours from there.

This role suits someone reliable, unhurried and genuinely interested in other people’s lives. Formal qualifications help but they are not the thing we screen hardest on.

Responsibilities

  • Provide personal care including showering, dressing, grooming and transfers
  • Support participants with meal preparation, shopping and household tasks
  • Assist with community access — appointments, social activities, work and study
  • Prompt and supervise medication in line with each participant’s health plan
  • Write clear, factual shift notes in our app before you finish
  • Report incidents and concerns promptly to your team leader
  • Work alongside families, coordinators and health professionals respectfully

Requirements

  • Current Australian driver’s licence and a comprehensively insured vehicle
  • NDIS Worker Screening Check and Working with Children Check (we help you apply and cover the cost)
  • First Aid and CPR certificate (we will fund this if you do not have one)
  • The right to work in Australia
  • Availability for at least three shifts a week, including one weekend shift a fortnight
  • Certificate III in Individual Support is desirable but not required

What we offer

  • $34.85 – $41.76 per hour plus superannuation, with penalty rates
  • Paid travel time between shifts and kilometres reimbursed
  • Paid two-day induction before your first shift
  • Ongoing training funded by us and completed in paid hours
  • Consistent participants so you build real relationships
  • A regional team leader reachable during every shift

We encourage applications from everyone

Including people with disability, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, people from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, and LGBTQIA+ people. If you need an adjustment at any stage of the process, tell us and we will arrange it.

Applications close 17 October 2026. We review as they arrive, so earlier is better.

posts.title: Marsden Street House
posts.content:
About this home

Marsden Street House is a single-storey brick home on a quiet residential street, renovated in 2024 to be fully accessible without looking like it. Neighbours on both sides have been there for years, and the corner shop knows everyone by name.

Three participants live here. Two have been housemates since the house opened and one room is now available. The house runs on a relaxed routine — most residents are out during the day at work, TAFE or community activities, and evenings are usually spent together over a shared meal.

Support is provided across the day with an active night worker on site. The team here has been stable for over two years.

Property overview

Features

  • Level entry from the street and off-street parking
  • Widened doorways throughout and a turning circle in every room
  • Accessible bathroom with a wet-room shower and grab rails
  • Ceiling hoist track in the available bedroom
  • Open-plan kitchen with a height-adjustable bench section
  • Covered outdoor area and a level, low-maintenance backyard
  • Reverse-cycle air conditioning in all bedrooms and the living area
  • NBN connected with wi-fi throughout the house

The available bedroom

Available Bedroom

The available room is at the rear of the house, facing the backyard. It measures 3.6m by 3.8m with a built-in wardrobe and a ceiling hoist track running to the ensuite.

  • Ceiling hoist track fitted
  • Ensuite with roll-in shower
  • Reverse-cycle air conditioning
  • Unfurnished — bring your own things

Accessibility

Fully wheelchair accessible

Level entry from the street and the garage, 950mm doorways throughout, turning circles in all bedrooms and living areas, a wet-room shower with fold-down seating and grab rails, and a height-adjustable kitchen bench section. An occupational therapist assessment is available on request.

Support at this home

Support is rostered from 6.00am to 10.00pm with two workers during peak periods, and an active night worker on site overnight. The house has a dedicated team leader who is on site three days a week.

Support hours are drawn from each resident’s individual SIL funding. During the matching process we will work through how your plan aligns with the roster here, and we will tell you plainly if it does not.

Location and nearby amenities

  • Parramatta station — 850m, step-free
  • Westfield Parramatta — 1.2km
  • Westmead Hospital — 3.4km
  • Parramatta Park — 600m, accessible paths
  • Community centre — 400m
